items.title: Paper Fold Limit
items.question: Starting with a single sheet, how many times can most people fold it in half before it becomes practically impossible?
items.correctExplanation: About 7. Each fold doubles the layers, so thickness explodes and the stack resists further folding.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7. Doubling is deceptively powerful: after only seven folds you already carry a thick wedge.
items.lessonContent:
Repeated doubling grows faster than intuition suggests.
Physical limits arrive sooner than expected.
Small exponents hide large effects.
Test a claim with a quick physical trial.
Share this: fold a sheet tonight and count each doubling.

items.title: Year of Sleep
items.question: Sleeping eight hours every night, how many hours of sleep does a person get in one non-leap year?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2920. Eight hours times 365 days gives the yearly total.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2920. Multiplying the daily amount by the days in a year is the direct route.
items.lessonContent:
Scale a daily habit to a yearly total.
Multiply rather than add.
Large totals reframe small routines.
Check the result against a known anchor.
Share this: total one nightly habit across a year.

items.title: Weeks in a Year
items.question: How many whole weeks fit into a non-leap year of 365 days?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 52. Seven times 52 is 364, leaving just one spare day.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 52. Dividing 365 by seven gives 52 with a remainder of one.
items.lessonContent:
Division with remainder clarifies cycles.
A near-miss remainder is worth noticing.
Calendars are arithmetic in disguise.
Check that weeks and days reconcile.
Share this: count how many weeks remain in this year.

items.title: Hand Overlaps
items.question: On a twelve-hour clock face, how many times do the hour and minute hands overlap?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 11. The overlap skips once in twelve hours, so the familiar twelve becomes eleven.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 11. The pair meets slightly less than once an hour, so one of the twelve possible points is missed.
items.lessonContent:
Continuous motion breaks neat hourly assumptions.
Relative speed, not absolute speed, decides meetings.
Off-by-one surprises are common in counting.
Verify with a quick diagram.
Share this: watch a clock and predict the next hand overlap.

items.title: Pizza Count
items.question: Twelve people each want three slices, and each pizza provides eight slices. How many pizzas must be ordered?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 5. Thirty-six slices are needed, and four pizzas give only thirty-two, so you round up.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Division leaves a remainder, and food cannot be served in fractions of a pizza.
items.lessonContent:
Round up when the supply comes in whole units.
Compute the total demand first.
Remainders matter in real logistics.
Check whether spare capacity is acceptable.
Share this: plan one purchase tonight by rounding up a remainder.

items.title: Decade of Books
items.question: Reading twelve books a year, how many books does a person finish in ten years?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 120. Twelve books a year across a decade gives one hundred and twenty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 120. Multiplying the yearly rate by ten years is the whole calculation.
items.lessonContent:
Small yearly habits compound across decades.
Multiply rates by the number of periods.
Long spans make modest rates impressive.
Check the total against your shelf.
Share this: project one yearly habit a decade ahead.

items.title: Snail Hour
items.question: A snail crawls one centimetre per minute. How many centimetres does it cover in one hour?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 60. One centimetre per minute over sixty minutes gives sixty centimetres.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 60. The rate and the time share a unit, so the multiplication is immediate.
items.lessonContent:
Match the rate's unit to the time span.
Simple rates scale linearly.
Compare slow rates with your own pace.
Convert units only when needed.
Share this: estimate how far a slow process gets in an hour.

items.title: Drips an Hour
items.question: A tap drips once every second. How many drips fall in one hour?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3600. One drip per second over sixty seconds and sixty minutes gives thirty-six hundred.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3600. Multiplying sixty by sixty converts seconds to an hourly total.
items.lessonContent:
Per-second rates grow quickly.
Convert time units in order.
Small leaks add up over hours.
Check the magnitude against intuition.
Share this: note how much one slow drip wastes in a day.

items.title: Candle Nights
items.question: A candle burns for four hours. How many candles are needed for seven evenings of three hours each?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 6. Twenty-one hours are needed, and five candles supply only twenty, so a sixth is required.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. The remainder after division forces a round up because candles are whole objects.
items.lessonContent:
Compute total demand before dividing.
Round up for indivisible supplies.
Leftover capacity is part of the cost.
Check whether partially used items can carry over.
Share this: plan one consumable purchase by totalling demand first.

items.title: Hens and Eggs
items.question: If each of six hens lays one egg every day, how many eggs do they lay in one week?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 42. Six hens times seven days gives forty-two eggs.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 42. Multiply the number of producers by the number of days.
items.lessonContent:
Multiply actors by periods to get output.
Keep the two counts separate.
Check with a smaller example first.
Units stay consistent throughout.
Share this: project one weekly output from a daily rate.

items.title: Spider Legs
items.question: Each spider has eight legs. How many legs do nine spiders have altogether?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 72. Eight legs times nine spiders gives seventy-two.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 72. Multiply the per-creature count by the number of creatures.
items.lessonContent:
Identify the unit count per object.
Multiply by the number of objects.
Simple multiplication scales cleanly.
Check the total by adding in groups.
Share this: count a repeated feature on several objects at once.

items.title: Clock Strikes
items.question: A clock strikes the hour once at one o'clock, twice at two, and so on. How many strikes does it make over twelve hours?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 78. Summing the numbers one through twelve gives seventy-eight.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 78. Pairing the ends of the series makes the sum quick: six pairs of thirteen.
items.lessonContent:
Series can be summed by pairing ends.
A tidy pattern replaces long addition.
Check a formula against a small case.
Recognise familiar number sequences.
Share this: sum one short sequence by pairing its ends.

items.title: Months with Twenty Eight
items.question: How many months of the year contain at least twenty-eight days?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 12. Every month reaches twenty-eight days, even those that continue further.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. The question asks which reach the mark, and all do, so the trick is in the wording.
items.lessonContent:
Read the exact claim before answering.
At least includes the boundary case.
Wording tricks target careless reading.
Restate the question in your own words.
Share this: check one 'at least' statement for its edge case tonight.

items.title: Cats and Mice
items.question: If three cats catch three mice in three minutes, how many mice do nine cats catch in nine minutes?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 27. Each cat catches one mouse every three minutes, so nine cats manage three rounds of nine.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 27. Scaling both the cats and the time multiplies the output rather than leaving it fixed.
items.lessonContent:
Find the per-unit rate first.
Then scale every factor independently.
Do not assume rates stay constant across changes.
Check the result with a smaller case.
Share this: compute a per-worker rate before scaling a team.

items.title: Trains in Two Hours
items.question: A train leaves the station every ten minutes. How many departures occur in two hours?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 12. One hundred and twenty minutes divided by ten gives twelve departures.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. Convert the hours to minutes and divide by the interval.
items.lessonContent:
Match the interval to the total time.
Division converts schedules into counts.
Watch for inclusive endpoints in counting.
Check with a short example.
Share this: count how many times an hourly event occurs today.

items.title: Chessboard Squares
items.question: Counting squares of every size, how many squares are there on a standard eight-by-eight chessboard?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 204. Summing squares of each size from one to eight gives two hundred and four.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 204. Counting only the smallest cells misses every larger square formed by their combination.
items.lessonContent:
Composite shapes hide inside grids.
Count size by size to avoid omissions.
Square counts follow a known pattern.
Sum the parts to verify the total.
Share this: count all squares in one tiled surface tonight.

items.title: Five Dozen
items.question: A crate holds five dozen eggs. How many eggs is that in total?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 60. A dozen is twelve, and five twelves make sixty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 60. Convert the dozen to twelve and multiply by five.
items.lessonContent:
Know common grouping units.
Convert groups to singles before multiplying.
Grouping speeds counting of many items.
Check the product for plausibility.
Share this: use one grouping unit to count something at home tonight.

items.title: Ten Days
items.question: Counting both the first and last day, how many days lie from January first to January tenth inclusive?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 10. Including both endpoints adds one to the simple difference.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. The word inclusive reminds you to count both ends rather than subtracting alone.
items.lessonContent:
Inclusive counting adds the endpoints.
Subtraction alone undercounts by one.
Read whether boundaries are included.
Test with a tiny range like days one to two.
Share this: count an inclusive range you use this week.

items.title: Rope Ladder
items.question: A rope ladder hangs with ten rungs spaced one foot apart. What is the distance from the top rung to the bottom rung?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 9. Ten rungs create nine gaps between them, so the span is nine feet.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 9. Counting rungs is not the same as counting the intervals between them.
items.lessonContent:
Count intervals, not objects, for distances.
Fence-post errors hide in simple counts.
Draw the arrangement to check.
Subtract one when counting spans.
Share this: count the gaps in one repeated row of objects.

items.title: Zeroes in a Million
items.question: How many zeroes are written in the number one million?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 6. One million is a one followed by six zeroes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Each power of ten adds a zero, and a million is ten to the sixth.
items.lessonContent:
Powers of ten map to counts of zeroes.
Named large numbers encode their magnitude.
Groups of three zeroes mark thousands.
Check by writing the number out.
Share this: write one large number and count its zero groups.

items.title: Five Minute Span
items.question: How many seconds are there in five minutes?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 300. Sixty seconds times five minutes gives three hundred.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 300. Multiply the per-minute count by the number of minutes.
items.lessonContent:
Scale a known unit to the span you need.
Multiplication suits repeated units.
Check the magnitude before moving on.
Convert only when the question demands it.
Share this: convert one short span into seconds at a glance.

items.title: Bucket of Cups
items.question: A bucket holds ten litres. How many half-litre cups can be filled from it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 20. Ten litres divided by half a litre gives twenty cups.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 20. Doubling the litre count is the quick way to handle half-litre units.
items.lessonContent:
Convert to matching units before dividing.
Halving the unit doubles the count.
Simple ratios answer capacity questions.
Check against a real container.
Share this: estimate how many small servings one container holds.

items.title: Coins for Weeks
items.question: Saving two coins every day, how many coins are collected in forty-five days?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 90. Two coins a day over forty-five days gives ninety.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 90. Multiply the daily rate by the number of days.
items.lessonContent:
Small daily rates accumulate steadily.
Multiply a rate by its duration.
Check the total against a shorter span.
Watch for a tempting round multiple.
Share this: project one small daily saving across a month.

items.title: Quarter Day
items.question: How many minutes make up one quarter of a day?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 360. A day holds 1440 minutes, and a quarter of that is three hundred and sixty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 360. Divide the daily minute count by four, or multiply six hours by sixty.
items.lessonContent:
Fractions of a day map to familiar spans.
Use either division or unit conversion.
Cross-check with two methods.
Keep a daily minute anchor handy.
Share this: name one activity that fills a quarter of your day.

items.title: Fast Clock
items.question: A clock gains five minutes every hour. How many minutes ahead is it after six hours?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 30. Five minutes per hour across six hours gives thirty minutes of drift.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 30. Multiply the hourly drift by the number of hours elapsed.
items.lessonContent:
Drift accumulates at a steady rate.
Track the rate separately from the reading.
Multiply by elapsed periods.
Check whether drift corrects or compounds.
Share this: estimate how far a steady error accumulates over a day.
